**Room Tone**

My brother asked me to record the kitchen before we sold the house.

“What do you want me to do in it?” I asked.

“Nothing,” he said. “That’s the point.”

He works in film. He told me that after a scene, the crew stands still and records thirty seconds of the room doing nothing. They use it later, to fill the gaps between bits of dialogue. If you leave the gaps truly silent, people notice.

I set my phone on the kitchen table. The refrigerator came on. A truck went past. I shifted in my chair and started over.

The third time, I made it to twenty-two seconds before the mail came through the slot. It was a grocery circular addressed to my mother, who had been dead for nine months. Peaches were ninety-nine cents a pound. She would have bought six, put them on the windowsill, and spent the next four days telling me which ones I was allowed to eat.

I left the recorder running while I folded the circular. I opened the utensil drawer, though we’d already packed the utensils. A single birthday candle rolled forward in the empty tray.

That evening I sent my brother the file.

“Sorry about the noise at the end,” I wrote.

He called me.

“Open the drawer again,” he said.

I did.

“Yeah,” he said. “I’d forgotten it does that.”

Halfway out, the drawer caught. You had to lift it a little. I’d done it without thinking, the way you step over a crack in the pavement on your own street.

“Wait,” I said. “I’ll do it wrong so you can hear.”
